meta.title: Who really said "Mirror, mirror on the wall"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Disney's Snow White never says it — the Queen says "Magic Mirror on the wall." The "Mirror, mirror" wording comes from Grimm, in English print by 1909.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Mirror, mirror on the wall'?
meta.ogDescription: The film's line is "Magic Mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?" And "Mirror, mirror" is older than Disney: it's Grimm in English, by 1909.

answer.label: Not quite — the film’s line is “Magic Mirror on the wall”
answer.authorDates: Ted Sears, Richard Creedon, Otto Englander, Dick Rickard, Earl Hurd, Merrill De Maris, Dorothy Ann Blank and Webb Smith · credited story, 1937
answer.sourceLine: In Disney’s Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) the Queen says “Magic Mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?” — both times she consults the mirror, and never “mirror, mirror.” The film carries a collective story credit to eight writers, so no single author of the sentence can honestly be named. The popular wording is not an invention either: it is a traditional English rendering of the Grimms’ Spieglein, Spieglein an der Wand, in print in English by 1909, decades before the film.

source.excerpt: “Magic Mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?”
trail: The transcribed film dialogue on Wikiquote ↗ gives the Queen’s line as “Magic Mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?” on both occasions she consults the mirror. The words “mirror, mirror” appear nowhere in it.

The Grimms’ German rhyme is „Spieglein, Spieglein an der Wand, wer ist die schönste im ganzen Land?“ — the text of the 1857 edition is at Wikisource ↗. The film is based on the Grimms’ tale, so the real question is which English rendering the public is quoting.

English translators disagreed. Margaret Hunt’s 1884 version has “Looking-glass, Looking-glass, on the wall, / Who in this land is the fairest of all?” (Wikisource ↗), but the Arthur Rackham–illustrated translation published in 1909 reads “Mirror, Mirror on the wall, / Who is fairest of us all?” (Project Gutenberg ↗). The popular phrase therefore predates the film.

No specialist has adjudicated this one: a site search of Quote Investigator ↗ returns no article on the line, and Wikiquote records no sourced discussion of the misquotation. The finding above rests directly on the transcript and the translations, not on a secondary chronology.
source.excerptNote: The Queen puts the question twice. The first time it runs exactly as above; the second time she interposes two words — “who now” — but still opens with “Magic Mirror on the wall.” Neither time does she say “mirror, mirror.” Transcribed on Wikiquote ↗.

author.name: Disney’s story team
author.heading: Who actually wrote the line
author.metaLine: Eight credited story writers · Walt Disney Productions, 1937
author.bio: The Magic Mirror’s verses have no single author. Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs carries a collective story credit — Ted Sears, Richard Creedon, Otto Englander, Dick Rickard, Earl Hurd, Merrill De Maris, Dorothy Ann Blank and Webb Smith — and the picture was developed through Disney’s story meetings rather than from one writer’s draft, so naming any one of them as the author of this line would be a guess. The characters who speak it are fictional: Queen Grimhilde, voiced by Lucille La Verne, addressing the Slave in the Magic Mirror, voiced by Moroni Olsen.

copyAttribution: The line is misquoted. In Disney's Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) the Queen says "Magic Mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?" — the words "mirror, mirror" are never spoken in the film. The familiar wording is older than the film: "Mirror, Mirror on the wall, / Who is fairest of us all?" is how the Grimms' rhyme reads in the Arthur Rackham–illustrated English translation published in 1909. Source: quotle.info

misattribution.heading: What actually went wrong
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here. The film is real, the scene is real, and the words are very nearly right. What drifted is the wording itself — and the assumption that Disney coined the phrase.

items.who: Disney’s Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937)
items.why: The Queen never says “mirror, mirror.” Both times she summons the Slave in the Magic Mirror she opens with “Magic Mirror on the wall” — see the transcribed dialogue on Wikiquote ↗.

items.who: The Brothers Grimm, in English translation
items.why: “Mirror, Mirror on the wall, / Who is fairest of us all?” is how the Grimms’ rhyme reads in the Arthur Rackham–illustrated translation published in 1909, decades before the film — full text at Project Gutenberg ↗. Disney did not coin the popular phrase; the film changed it.

items.who: “… who’s the fairest of them all?”
items.why: The familiar tail matches none of the three texts on this page. The film says “the fairest one of all” (Wikiquote ↗); the 1909 translation says “fairest of us all”; Margaret Hunt’s 1884 version says “the fairest of all” (Wikisource ↗). The popular sentence is a composite, not a transcript.

misattribution.truthLine: What the Queen actually says is “Magic Mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?” (Wikiquote ↗) — and the “Mirror, mirror” everyone remembers is older than the film, standing in English editions of Grimm by 1909 (Project Gutenberg ↗).

context.heading: Why this one drifted
lead: Most famous misquotations put words into a stranger’s mouth. This one is odder: the misquote is a real line, from a real book, that the film simply did not use. Where the English translations double the word — “Mirror, Mirror on the wall” — the film names the object instead: “Magic Mirror on the wall.”

So the public invented nothing. It remembered the printed fairy tale and filed the memory under the film it saw, and the two versions have been quietly overwriting each other ever since. The result is a sentence faithful to neither: familiar, endlessly repeated, and not a transcript of anything.
detailsBody: The Grimms’ German uses a diminutive, Spieglein — roughly ‘little mirror’ — doubled for the rhyme, and English translators have handled it in very different ways. Margaret Hunt’s 1884 version reaches for ‘Looking-glass, Looking-glass’; the 1909 Rackham edition uses ‘Mirror, Mirror’; the film uses neither. There is no single ‘correct’ English rhyme to drift away from — only a film line that is documented exactly.

Quote Investigator has not published on this line, so there is no specialist chronology to defer to here. Everything on this page rests on the film transcript and on the translations themselves, each of which is linked below and can be read in full.
context.pull: The misquote is a real line — just not from the film everyone credits.

The film's story credit is Ted Sears, Richard Creedon, Otto Englander, Dick Rickard, Earl Hurd, Merrill De Maris, Dorothy Ann Blank and Webb Smith; it premiered 21 December 1937 at the Carthay Circle Theatre with US general release 4 February 1938; produced by Walt Disney Productions, distributed by RKO Radio Pictures; based on the Brothers Grimm tale.

The English text reads "Mirror, Mirror on the wall, / Who is fairest of us all?" and its front matter states it was originally published in 'Grimm's Fairy Tales. Illustrated by Arthur Rackham' 1909, and re-issued separately 1920.
